Ana boarded the train carrying a canvas bag and a folded coat. She placed the bag beneath her seat, arranged the coat beside her, and checked the destination printed on her ticket. The train passed warehouses, apartment blocks, and fields divided by narrow roads. She opened a book and read several pages before setting it on her lap. At a station, passengers entered with suitcases while others stepped onto the platform. Ana moved her coat to make room for a woman who sat beside her. Later, she walked to the dining carriage and bought a sandwich and a bottle of water. She ate at her seat, folded the wrapper, and put it in the bin near the door. Outside, fields gave way to wooded slopes and scattered houses. As daylight faded, the carriage lights came on. Ana returned to her book while the train continued toward the next station.

Lukas boarded the train with a small suitcase and placed it on the rack above his seat. He took off his coat, folded it across his knees, and looked through the window as the platform passed out of view. Beyond the station, warehouses gave way to fields and rows of bare trees. He opened a book and read several pages before putting a ticket on the table for the conductor. At the next stop, passengers entered with bags and took seats along the aisle. Lukas ate a sandwich from a paper wrapper, drank water, and brushed the crumbs into the empty wrapper. During the afternoon, the train passed towns, bridges, and stretches of farmland. He walked to the carriage door, stood there briefly, and returned to his seat. When the overhead lights came on, he put his book away and checked the station names displayed above the aisle.

Lukas boarded the train beneath a red station canopy, carrying a brick-red suitcase and a folded map. His seat had burgundy upholstery, and a crimson curtain hung beside the window. As the train crossed the outskirts, red roofs passed between warehouses and rows of rust-colored fencing. He placed his ticket on the scarlet tablecloth and opened a book with a maroon cover. At noon, an attendant brought tomato soup in a white bowl on a red tray. Lukas ate, turned several pages, and watched reddish fields extend beneath the afternoon sky. The journey continued through stations marked by vermilion columns and red enamel platform numbers. He walked along the corridor’s wine-red carpet, filled his bottle, and returned to his seat. By evening, red lamps illuminated the carriage while muted scarlet reflections crossed the glass. Lukas packed his book beside the crimson map case as the train entered another stretch of countryside.

The overnight train carried Lukas across three borders, past freight yards and fields silvered by frost. He had booked the journey when the hospital called, packing a clean shirt and the wooden bird his father had carved for him. All evening, he watched the carriage clock and calculated the hours remaining. Near dawn, his phone vibrated against the window ledge. A nurse told him his father had died twenty minutes earlier. Lukas kept the phone pressed to his ear after the call ended. Outside, a station platform slid past, its benches empty beneath the lamps. He took the wooden bird from his bag and rubbed its chipped wing until his thumb grew sore. The shirt would stay folded now. There would be no bedside chair, no hand reaching across the blanket. When the conductor asked for his ticket, Lukas searched every pocket twice, though it lay on his knee. He could not make his fingers close around it.

Leila boarded the train before sunrise and placed a notebook beside the window. The route covered 1,440 kilometers, and the timetable listed 18 hours aboard. She divided 1,440 by 18 and wrote 80 kilometers per hour as the overall average. After the first stretch, she subtracted 180 from 1,440, leaving 1,260 kilometers. Fields passed behind the glass while she counted the carriage windows: 12 on each side, multiplied by 2, made 24. At the next station, 17 passengers entered her carriage and 8 departed; she added 17 to the previous count of 26, then subtracted 8 from 43, arriving at 35. She measured six equal sections on her route map, dividing 1,260 by 6 to label each section 210 kilometers. Through the afternoon and into darkness, she updated distances beneath the overhead lamp. When the train reached its final platform, she closed the notebook and stepped down.

The overnight train carried Ana across flat winter fields toward the coastal city, its windows streaked with rain. She had packed a clean nightgown for her mother and a jar of the peach preserves they always shared after hospital visits. Seven hours into the journey, her phone lit up. A nurse told her that her mother had stopped breathing before dawn. Ana kept the phone against her ear after the call ended, listening to the empty line until the screen went dark. Outside, stations passed without stopping. She unscrewed the jar, then tightened the lid again; there would be nobody waiting to complain that she had used too much sugar. Her throat worked, but she could not swallow. She folded the nightgown into smaller and smaller squares on her lap. When the conductor asked for her ticket, she held out the hospital visiting pass instead, and watched his hand remain open.

Lukas had spent fourteen hours aboard the night train as it crossed the mountains toward the coast. By midnight, the carriage held only him and a sleeping passenger beneath a gray coat. Then the brakes screamed. His cup slid off the table, and the windows flashed with sparks. The train stopped halfway across a bridge, its last wheels striking the rails with a sound like dropped hammers. Outside, a stone support cracked and disappeared into the river.

“Stay seated,” the conductor said from the doorway.

But the floor was already tilting. Lukas gripped the armrests until his fingertips went white. His heart battered his ribs; each breath stopped somewhere high in his chest. He pictured the carriage breaking loose, the black water sealing every window. When the sleeping passenger stirred, Lukas crawled toward him, unable to stand. Beneath them, metal groaned again. He reached for the man’s coat and pulled him toward the adjoining carriage.

Leila boarded the train before sunrise, carrying a red canvas bag and a ticket printed with a crimson border. Her seat had burgundy upholstery, and a scarlet curtain hung beside the wide window. She placed a red notebook on the table and copied the station names from the route map. For several hours, brick warehouses and red tiled roofs passed beyond the glass. At midday, she ate rice from a maroon container while another passenger unfolded a newspaper with a red masthead. The train crossed a plain where rust colored soil lay between rows of green crops. Leila turned three pages, adjusted the scarlet curtain, and checked the carriage clock. By evening, sunset cast red light across her notebook and the empty cup beside it. She spent the remaining hours listing distances in red pencil. After midnight, she took her canvas bag from beneath the burgundy seat and stepped onto the platform under ruby colored lamps.

Leila’s train crossed the flat countryside beneath a pale afternoon sky, six hours from the city where her sister lived. She had paid extra for a window seat and kept the ticket folded beside her water bottle. At the next station, a conductor ordered her into the corridor so another traveler could take her place. She showed him the printed seat number. He barely glanced at it. “This seat is needed.” The other traveler settled in, spreading a coat across the cushion Leila had warmed for hours. Heat climbed her neck. Her fingers crushed the ticket until its edges bit her palm. There were empty seats farther down, but the conductor blocked her return with one arm. Apparently, her money counted less than someone else’s convenience. Leila planted her suitcase across the aisle and demanded a written explanation, each word clipped and hard. She would not spend the remaining journey standing beside the toilets.

Ana’s train crossed the plains beneath a pale morning sky, its windows striped with dust. By the ninth hour, her knees pressed against the seat ahead and the sandwich in her bag had gone warm. She had paid extra for a sleeper berth, but the conductor had given it to a passenger whose ticket cost less. When she showed her receipt, he folded it without reading and told her to remain seated. Through the corridor doorway, she watched the passenger stretch beneath clean sheets. Heat climbed her neck. Her fingers tightened around the receipt until its edges cut into her palm. Nine hours of rattling, and tonight she would sleep upright because someone had decided she could be pushed aside. She stood, blocked the conductor’s trolley with her suitcase, and held out the crumpled paper. “Read it.” When he reached for her case, she planted both hands on its handle and refused to move.

Lukas sat beside a scratched window as the train crossed its seventh hour of farmland and industrial towns. His reserved seat number matched the ticket tucked beneath his thumb. At the next stop, a conductor arrived with a passenger carrying two expensive suitcases and told Lukas to move into the corridor. Lukas showed his reservation. The conductor glanced at it, then waved it aside; the passenger had paid an upgrade fee. Every other seat was occupied. Lukas stood between the toilets while his former seat disappeared behind a drawn curtain. Heat climbed his neck. He folded the ticket until its edges cut into his palm. Six more hours, and they expected him to stand because someone else could pay twice. When the conductor passed again, Lukas planted his suitcase across the narrow aisle and held out the crumpled reservation. His jaw ached from clenching it. He would not step aside this time.

Ana boarded the coastal train before sunrise, carrying a canvas bag and a timetable printed with small harbor symbols. The railway followed the seawall for several hours, passing fishing boats, tidal flats, and rows of nets drying beside the ocean. She placed a bottle of water on the table while waves crossed the narrow strip of view beneath the window. By noon, the train had rounded three bays where gulls stood among mussel beds exposed by the falling tide. Ana ate bread and sliced cucumber as a cargo ship moved parallel to the carriage beyond the coastline. During an afternoon stop, she walked along the platform, which faced a harbor of ferries and floating ropes. The journey continued past salt marshes, oyster farms, and channels marked by buoys. After sunset, Ana checked the remaining stations while offshore lights outlined ships traveling across the dark seawater.

Lukas boarded the morning train beside a harbor where fishing boats rested against floating pontoons. His route followed the coastline for fourteen hours, passing beaches, tidal flats, and channels marked by red buoys. He placed his bag beneath the seat and watched seawater slide between rows of wooden pilings. Beyond the window, cormorants stood on rocks while small waves covered and uncovered their lower edges. At a coastal station, a vendor carried baskets of bread past a mural of whales. Lukas bought a roll and ate it as the train crossed an estuary on a steel bridge. The afternoon timetable included several stops near ferry terminals, salt marshes, and sheds stacked with lobster pots. He read three pages of a booklet about local tides, then returned it to his bag. After sunset, lights from ships appeared offshore, and the train continued beside the sea toward the final coastal platform.

Leila’s train crossed the plains through the night, its windows reflecting rows of seats and the overhead luggage racks. She had packed two oranges, a wool scarf, and the photograph her mother had requested for the bedside table. By morning, the carriage smelled of coffee, and twelve stations still lay between her and the hospital. At a signal stop, her phone rang. She listened while a nurse explained that her mother had died before dawn. Leila kept one hand around an orange until her thumbnail broke the skin. Juice ran into her cuff. Outside, a worker walked beside the tracks, carrying a hammer; somewhere ahead, passengers were buying tickets and checking clocks. She opened the photograph, then turned it face down on her lap. All those miles remained, but there was no longer anyone waiting at their end. When the train moved again, she pressed the scarf against her mouth and bent forward, unable to swallow.

Ana traveled north on a train that crossed three regions before reaching the coast. She opened a notebook beside the window and recorded the journey in numbers. The first stretch covered 168 kilometers and the second covered 147; she added 168 + 147 = 315 kilometers. The full route measured 924 kilometers, so she subtracted 924 − 315 = 609 kilometers remaining. Between stations, she counted 24 trackside posts in each of 7 groups and wrote 24 × 7 = 168 posts. She divided the scheduled 18 hours into 6 equal sections: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 hours per section. At the next stop, passengers entered and placed bags overhead. Ana moved her notebook to let a sleeve pass. Later, she counted 36 windows across 3 carriages and calculated 36 ÷ 3 = 12 windows per carriage. Fields gave way to warehouses, then fields again. She closed the notebook as the train continued north.

Leila boarded the train in the morning and placed her bag on the rack above her seat. She took a book from its side pocket, opened it at the bookmark, and read while the platform slid past the window. Beyond the station, rows of houses gave way to fields and low warehouses. A conductor checked her ticket and continued down the aisle. Leila closed the book, drank some water, and unwrapped a sandwich. At the next stop, several passengers left and others entered carrying bags and folded coats. Through the afternoon, she alternated between reading and looking outside. The train passed bridges, farm buildings, and stations with benches beneath their signs. She walked to the carriage door to stretch her legs, then returned to her seat. When the lamps outside came on, she put the book away and checked the destination printed on her ticket.

Ana’s train crossed the northern plains through the night, its windows reflecting rows of seats beneath yellow ceiling lamps. By morning, she had counted twelve stations and eaten the last sandwich from her bag. Beyond the glass, fields gave way to steep slopes and narrow bridges. Then a sharp crack passed beneath her feet. Her cup jumped off the table, and the carriage began gathering speed downhill. A conductor hurried through the aisle, pulling uselessly at each emergency handle. “Stay in your seats,” he said. Ana gripped the armrests until her fingers ached. Ahead, through the open carriage doors, she could see a curve approaching above a deep ravine. The wheels shrieked, but the train did not slow. She pressed her shoes against the floor, as though she could hold it back herself. Her mouth dried. She pictured the empty chair at her kitchen table and could not make herself look away from the curve.

Lukas boarded the train at 06:20 and placed his bag beneath the seat. The route covered 840 kilometers, and he divided 840 by 7 to calculate an average of 120 kilometers per hour. In his notebook, he added 135 and 225, obtaining 360 kilometers for the first two sections. He subtracted 360 from 840 and recorded 480 kilometers remaining. Beyond the window, fields gave way to warehouses, then returned between stations. Lukas multiplied 18 carriages by 64 seats and wrote 1,152 as the total seating capacity. At the next stop, several passengers entered while others stepped onto the platform. He counted 24 fence posts along one stretch, then divided 24 by 3 to make 8 groups. The train continued through a tunnel. Lukas folded the route map, drank water, and checked the distance markers until the final station appeared beyond a row of signal lamps.

Leila’s train crossed the plains beneath a pale morning sky, its windows striped with last night’s rain. She had been aboard for nineteen hours, with another six between her and the hospital where her mother lay. Her phone had lost its signal beyond the mountains. She kept turning it over beside an untouched sandwich, watching tunnels swallow the landscape and release it again. Near a river bridge, the screen lit up. The operation had worked. Her mother was awake and asking when she would arrive. Leila read the message three times, then pressed the phone against her chest. A laugh burst out of her, startling the passenger across the aisle. She bought tea and two pastries, offering one to him with both hands. Fields flashed gold outside. For the remaining miles, her feet tapped beneath the table, and she rehearsed walking through the ward door, hearing her mother complain about the late train.

Leila boarded the morning train beside a harbor where fishing boats rested above their reflections. Her ticket covered twelve hours along the coast, with several stops near tidal inlets. She placed her bag beneath the seat and opened a timetable printed with a map of the shoreline. Beyond the window, seawater filled channels between sandbanks, and gulls stood beside oyster beds. The train passed a freight yard stacked with containers from ships anchored offshore. At noon, Leila ate bread and cheese while waves folded onto a narrow beach below the tracks. An attendant checked her ticket as the coastline curved toward a port of cranes and ferries. Through the afternoon, salt marshes alternated with stretches of open sea, where small sails crossed the horizon. Leila recorded each station in a notebook beside the coastline map. After sunset, the train reached its final platform overlooking a basin of seawater lined with moored boats.

Ana boarded the train before sunrise and placed her red suitcase beneath a seat upholstered in faded crimson cloth. A burgundy curtain covered half the window, and the aisle carpet carried narrow scarlet stripes between rows of seats. For the first hundred miles, she read a timetable printed with red headings and marked each station with a vermilion pencil. Outside, brick warehouses gave way to fields, where red roofs appeared at intervals beside the tracks. At noon, she ate bread and sliced tomatoes from a rust-colored tin, then folded her ruby napkin into quarters. The train continued through several provinces while reddish sunlight crossed her table and shifted along the carriage wall. At intermediate stops, passengers entered with maroon bags, red coats, and parcels tied with crimson string. After dusk, Ana closed her book with its scarlet bookmark in place; her red suitcase remained beneath the seat as the journey continued.

Ana’s train crossed the northern plains beneath a pale sky, its windows streaked with dust from fourteen hours of travel. On her lap lay a small knitted cardigan, one sleeve still unfinished. She had worked on it through two stations, a tunnel, and the long stretch where the dining car ran out of coffee. Her daughter’s baby had arrived three weeks early, and every delay meant another hour before Ana could hold her. Near dusk, the train stopped outside the final station. Ana gripped her knitting needles. Then the signals changed, and the carriage rolled forward. On the platform, her daughter stood beside a stroller, waving both arms. Ana laughed so suddenly that the passenger across from her looked up. She stuffed the unfinished cardigan into her bag and hurried down the aisle, her cheeks aching from her widening smile. There they were. She had crossed all those miles, and there they were.

The overnight train carried Lukas through wheat fields, mountain tunnels, and towns whose platforms lay beneath yellow lamps. He had spent fourteen hours beside the window, checking the same message whenever the carriage found a signal. His application still showed as pending. Across his knees rested a folder of drawings, its corners softened by months of revisions. Beyond the next pass waited the city where he hoped to study, if he could afford it. Then his phone vibrated. The scholarship committee had accepted him, with tuition and housing covered. He read the message once, twice, then pressed his palm against his mouth. A laugh escaped between his fingers. His shoulders lifted; his feet tapped beneath the seat. He wanted to show somebody, everybody. Instead, he held the screen toward the elderly passenger opposite him, who smiled. Outside, the mountains opened around a broad river. Lukas unfolded his drawings and began sketching the view.

Leila’s train crossed the mountain plateau on the second night of a journey that had begun beside the sea. She had folded her coat beneath her head when a metallic bang jolted her upright. Outside, sparks streamed past the windows. The carriage rocked, and a suitcase slid from the overhead rack into the aisle. Then the lights went out. Through the glass, she saw the curve ahead and, beyond it, a railway bridge with a section missing. She pulled the emergency handle until its casing cracked, but the wheels kept hammering beneath her feet. Her mouth dried; her heartbeat thudded against her ribs. She pictured the carriage tipping into the black ravine and could not finish the thought. A passenger crawled toward the connecting door. Leila followed on trembling knees, gripping seat legs whenever the floor lurched. Somewhere ahead, brakes shrieked. She counted the impacts beneath her palms, waiting for the last one.

Carlos boarded the train before sunrise and placed his bag on the rack above his seat. He took a timetable from his coat pocket, unfolded it, and laid it beside the window. Beyond the glass, platform lamps passed out of view, followed by warehouses and rows of houses. He opened a book and read until the train reached a station outside the city. A passenger entered the carriage carrying a paper cup. Carlos moved his timetable onto his lap and continued reading. Later, he walked to the dining carriage, bought a sandwich and a bottle of water, and returned to his seat. Fields gave way to wooded slopes, then to another stretch of towns. During the afternoon, he put the book away and watched roads running alongside the tracks. As evening arrived, he checked the station names on the timetable and zipped his coat. The train continued through the countryside.

Beatriz reached the municipal pitch before the amateur football match began. She placed her bag beside the bench, tied her boots, and walked onto the grass with the other players. The referee checked the nets and signaled for the teams to take their positions. Beatriz stood near the touchline while a teammate passed the ball across the center of the field. She received it, turned toward the opposing half, and sent it along the ground to another player. Play continued through several passes, a throw-in, and a goal kick. During a pause, she adjusted her socks and drank from a bottle beside the bench. The grass had patches of bare soil near each goalmouth. After the match resumed, Beatriz moved between the touchline and midfield, making short passes when the ball reached her. At the final whistle, she collected her bag and left through the open gate.

On Sunday afternoon, Beatriz played midfield in an amateur football match on a muddy pitch behind the community hall. Ten minutes from the end, she slipped between two defenders and reached a loose ball inside the penalty area. A boot hooked her ankle, sending her face-first into the mud. The referee waved play on. Moments later, he awarded the opposing team a penalty when their striker stumbled over untouched grass. Beatriz stood with grit between her teeth and watched him point to the spot. Her neck burned. She had spent the match absorbing elbows while his whistle stayed silent. “You saw that,” she said. He showed her a yellow card without meeting her eyes. Her fingers curled so tightly that her nails pressed crescents into her palms. She wanted to tear the card from his hand. Instead, she backed away, jaw locked, and drove her next clearance hard enough to sting her foot.

Carlos sat beside the window as the overnight train crossed its third mountain range beneath a moonless sky. He had spent sixteen hours watching fields become foothills, then cliffs, with his suitcase wedged beneath his knees. Near midnight, a sharp crack came from under the carriage. His cup slid off the table. The train gathered speed instead of slowing for the curve ahead, and the conductor hurried past, pulling uselessly at a lever beside the door. Carlos pressed his palms against the seat. Beyond the glass, sparks streamed backward along the wheels; farther down the track, a signal glowed red above a narrow bridge. His throat tightened until he could barely swallow. He pictured the carriage leaving the rails, the suitcase tumbling after him into the black ravine. When the lights went out, he dropped between the seats and covered his head, counting each violent jolt, waiting for the next one not to land.

Carlos rode the overnight train across the plains, with eighteen hours remaining before the coast. At each station, he checked the ticket tucked inside his shirt pocket. He had paid extra for a sleeper after three weeks of double shifts. Near midnight, a conductor informed him that his berth had been given to another passenger and pointed toward a narrow seat beside the lavatory. Through the compartment door, Carlos saw the passenger hand the conductor folded bills.

“That berth is mine,” he said.

The conductor tapped a sign about crew discretion and walked away. Heat climbed Carlos’s neck. He followed, gripping his ticket so tightly that its edge cut his thumb. Every wheel joint hammered the same thought into him: his money counted less because he had no extra cash to slip into a palm. He planted himself outside the occupied compartment, jaw locked, and pressed the call button again and again until footsteps returned.

Beatriz stood beside the touchline during an amateur football match and kept the match sheet on a clipboard. She counted 8 players near the benches and 14 on the pitch, then wrote 8 + 14 = 22. The referee had scheduled two halves of 35 minutes, so she calculated 2 × 35 = 70 minutes of play. After 19 minutes, she subtracted 70 − 19 = 51 minutes remaining. At the interval, she counted 24 orange slices and divided them among 12 players: 24 ÷ 12 = 2 slices each. She also recorded 6 corners for one side and 3 for the other, making 6 + 3 = 9 corners altogether. During the second half, Beatriz retrieved a ball from beside the fence and returned it to the nearest player. The match ended at 2–2. She added 2 + 2 = 4 goals, capped her pen, and carried the clipboard toward the gate.

Beatriz arrived at the coastal football pitch while the tide covered the lower steps of the harbor wall. She placed her bottle beside a bench facing the seawater and joined the other amateur players near the center circle. Beyond the touchline, fishing boats moved between buoys, and gulls stood along the railing. The match began with a short pass to her feet as small waves reached the strip of sand below the pitch. She carried the ball toward the harbor end, then passed it to a player whose socks bore a pattern of blue fish. At halftime, Beatriz drank water while a ferry crossed the bay behind the goalposts. The second half produced two goals, several throw-ins, and a ball retrieved from beside a basket of oyster shells. When the final whistle sounded, she collected her bottle and walked along the coastline with the other players.

Carlos sat beside the window as the overnight train crossed a plain of harvested fields. Above his seat, a paper bag held two oranges and the wool scarf he had bought for his mother. He had three connections left before reaching her town, and he kept checking the timetable folded inside his ticket. At dawn, his phone rang. A nurse told him his mother had died an hour earlier; she had asked whether his train was running on time. After the call ended, he held the phone against his ear until the screen went dark. Outside, station platforms slid past, crowded with people carrying breakfast and newspapers. He took the scarf from its bag and spread it over his knees. There was no longer anyone waiting to try it on. When the conductor requested his ticket, Carlos searched the same pocket repeatedly, his fingers trembling, unable to remember what he was looking for.

Carlos boarded the red train before dawn and placed his burgundy suitcase beneath a seat upholstered in scarlet fabric. A crimson ticket lay beside his paper timetable, which listed fourteen hours of travel across the plain. Beyond the window, red brick warehouses gave way to fields bordered by rusty fences and occasional vermilion sheds. He ate bread from a red tin, folded the paper wrapping, and returned the tin to his bag. At each station, passengers crossed platforms tiled with reddish stone while porters moved maroon carts between the carriages. By noon, red curtains filtered the daylight into narrow bands across his sleeves and the tabletop. Carlos read several chapters of a book with a cherry-red cover, then recorded mile markers in a notebook. The train continued past clay banks, copper-colored roofs, and rows of red freight containers. After sunset, he collected his burgundy suitcase beneath the carriage’s red ceiling lamps and stepped onto the final platform.

Carlos boarded the train at six and placed his notebook beside the window. The journey covered 840 kilometers, and he divided 840 by 70 to obtain 12 hours of travel. After the first section, he added 135 kilometers to 145 kilometers and wrote 280 kilometers beneath the two entries. He subtracted 280 from 840, leaving 560 kilometers ahead. Outside, fields passed between rows of poles. Carlos counted 18 poles in each of 4 stretches and multiplied 18 by 4 to get 72. At a station, several passengers entered while others stepped onto the platform. He opened a container holding 24 crackers, divided 24 by 6, and arranged 4 crackers in each row. Later, he added 7 tunnels to the earlier 5, recording 12 tunnels altogether. The train continued through farmland and cuttings. Carlos turned another page, noted the kilometer marker, and returned the pencil to its clip.

Bruno played right back in an amateur football match on a muddy municipal pitch beside the railway. With ten minutes left, he intercepted a pass and drove the ball upfield. An opponent hooked his ankle from behind, sending him face-first into the turf. The referee waved play on. When Bruno scrambled up and caught the opponent’s sleeve, the whistle finally blew against him. “Free kick,” the referee said, pointing toward Bruno’s goal. Bruno’s jaw locked. Heat climbed his neck as the opponent smirked and brushed mud from his socks. So that was how it worked: a shove for one side, a whistle for the other. Bruno pressed his tongue against a split lip and tasted blood. He kicked a clod hard enough to scatter it across the touchline. At the next tackle, he planted himself squarely, shoulders rigid, and demanded that the referee watch both players this time.

Beatriz played goalkeeper on a municipal pitch where two amateur football teams competed beneath a row of floodlights. By halftime, mud covered her socks, and the score remained level. During a corner, a defender collided with the goalpost. The frame tilted, then settled with a metallic crack. Beatriz glanced down and saw that its base had pulled free of the ground. Before she could move, another player backed into the upright. The crossbar swung toward her head. Her knees locked. Breath stopped halfway up her throat, and the shouts around her became distant, thin sounds. She pictured the weight striking her skull and her mother waiting beside an unanswered phone. Dropping flat, she crawled through the mud as the frame crashed inches behind her boots. Hands pulled her clear. Even after the referee stopped the match, she could not stand; she kept staring at the crossbar, certain it would somehow move again.

Carlos’s train crossed a flat stretch of farmland beneath the pale light of an October morning. He had been traveling for thirty hours, with another six still printed on his ticket. In his coat pocket lay a photograph of his daughter beside the hospital bed where she had spent most of the summer. He checked his phone whenever the signal returned, then watched the tracks unspool beyond the window. Near dusk, a video arrived. His daughter stood between two nurses, released their hands, and took five small steps across a room. Carlos played it again. Then again. His mouth opened into a grin so wide his cheeks ached. He pressed the phone against his chest and laughed, startling the passenger opposite him. Outside, station lamps began sliding past. For the first time, he pictured his arrival clearly: her crossing the platform toward him, and himself setting down his suitcase to catch her.

Carlos boarded the coastal train beside a harbor where fishing boats moved between rows of buoys. His journey lasted two days, with the railway following beaches, tidal flats, and seawalls for most of its route. Through the window, he watched waves fold onto sand while gulls crossed above the water. He placed his bag beneath the seat and unfolded a timetable printed with the names of seaside stations. At noon, he ate bread and cheese as the train passed salt marshes threaded with narrow channels. Beyond a stretch of dunes, cargo ships marked the horizon, their outlines changing as the tracks curved inland and returned to the coast. He slept after sunset while moonlight lay across an estuary beside the railway. The next morning, oyster beds appeared beyond the glass, followed by piers and anchored sailboats. Carlos left the train at a terminal overlooking the sea and carried his bag along the waterfront.

Bruno arrived at the recreation ground with his boots in a cloth bag. He sat on a bench, changed his shoes, and joined the other players beside the touchline. Someone placed a ball near the center circle while the referee checked the nets. Bruno took his position on the right side of midfield. When play began, he followed the ball across the pitch and received a pass near the halfway line. He controlled it with his foot, then sent it to a teammate beside the sideline. The match continued with short passes, throw-ins, and occasional stoppages. During the interval, Bruno drank water and adjusted his socks. He returned to the same position and moved between the center circle and the wing. After the final whistle, he shook hands with nearby players, collected his bag from the bench, and walked toward the gate.

On Sunday afternoon, Beatriz stood beside the chalk line of a muddy football pitch while two amateur teams warmed up. She wore her father’s faded jersey beneath her coat and held the whistle he had used for twenty years. Since his funeral, she had kept this match circled on the kitchen calendar. At halftime, a groundskeeper handed her an envelope from the council. The pitch had been sold; Monday’s fences would mark the beginning of a car park. She read the notice twice while players drank from plastic bottles around her. Her fingers tightened until the paper split along its fold. Here, her father had taught her to pass, counted her goals, and waited after every defeat. By the final whistle, she could barely swallow. She stayed after everyone left, pressing her shoe into the centre spot, trying to leave a mark that the machinery might somehow miss.

The amateur football match took place on a muddy school pitch beneath a row of flickering floodlights. Beatriz had spent most of the second half chasing passes that skipped beyond her boots. With two minutes remaining, her team trailed by one goal, and the spectators huddled beside the touchline. Then a teammate intercepted a clearance and rolled the ball into her path. Beatriz took one touch, slipped past a defender, and struck with her weaker foot. The ball hit the inside of the post and crossed the line. Before she could catch her breath, her team won possession again. This time she sent a low pass across the goalmouth, and a teammate tapped it home. Beatriz sprang upward, both arms stretched over her head. Laughter burst from her as muddy shirts surrounded her. They had done it. At the final whistle, she ran toward the touchline, grinning so widely that her cheeks ached.

On Sunday afternoon, Bruno stood beside the touchline of a muddy football pitch behind the village school. His father occupied his usual folding chair near the halfway line, a blanket across his knees. In the final minutes, Bruno scored his first goal of the season and turned toward that chair. It was empty. Beyond the fence, two paramedics knelt beside someone in a familiar brown coat. Bruno ran off the pitch without waiting for the whistle. A teammate caught his arm, but he pulled free. At the hospital, a doctor spoke quietly, and Bruno kept looking at the mud drying on his socks. His father had come despite the chest pains because he had promised not to miss another match. That evening, Bruno found the folding chair in the teammate’s car. He carried it home, opened it in the kitchen, and sat on the floor beside it until morning.

On Sunday afternoon, two amateur football teams played on a muddy pitch behind the village hall. Bruno had spent most of the match chasing passes that skipped beyond his boots. With the score level and minutes remaining, he nearly asked to come off. Then a teammate intercepted the ball and sent it rolling into the open space ahead of him. Bruno ran, caught it with his left foot, and struck before the goalkeeper could reach him. The ball clipped the post and crossed the line. For a heartbeat, he stood motionless, checking the net. Then his mouth opened into a grin so wide his cheeks ached. He sprinted toward his teammates, arms spread, and collided with a tangle of muddy shirts. Laughter kept escaping him between breaths. He had scored. His clumsy left foot had actually done it. Even after the final whistle, he bounced on his toes, replaying that clean strike with every step toward the changing rooms.

Bruno arrived at the amateur football ground wearing a red shirt, crimson socks, and boots with scarlet laces. Beside the touchline, red canvas chairs stood beneath a burgundy awning, where several spectators arranged cups of red juice. He placed his cherry-red bag beside a brick-red bench and joined the other players on the grass. A teammate rolled the ball toward him, its white panels marked with faded red printing. Bruno passed it across the center circle while the referee, dressed in dark red, checked his watch. Above the pitch, the late sunlight cast a reddish tint over the clubhouse windows and rust-colored roof. The match continued with short passes, throw-ins, and occasional pauses beside the red corner flags. At halftime, he drank from a red bottle and adjusted his crimson socks. After the final whistle, Bruno collected his scarlet jacket, folded it into his bag, and walked past the red gate toward the road.

Bruno played in an amateur football match on a grass pitch beside the harbor, where fishing boats shifted with the tide. Beyond the touchline, small waves spread across a narrow strip of shingle. He wore a blue shirt and passed the ball toward a teammate while gulls crossed above the seawall. The opposing side moved upfield, their boots pressing into turf bordered by patches of coastal sand. Bruno intercepted a low pass and sent it sideways as a ferry traveled between the offshore buoys. At halftime, he drank water near a fence hung with nets drying from seawater. The second half began while the tide covered another row of stones along the beach. He took a throw-in facing the harbor cranes, then returned to his position beside the coastal path. The match ended at one goal each, and Bruno carried his boots past the moored boats.

Beatriz arrived at the amateur football pitch wearing a red jersey, scarlet socks, and boots with crimson laces. Beside the touchline, red canvas bags rested beneath a burgundy bench, where substitutes arranged their water bottles. She placed a ruby-colored bottle near the corner flag and joined the players gathering around a red practice ball. The referee checked the teams against a clipboard covered in red plastic, then started the match. Beatriz received a pass, carried the ball across the midfield stripe, and sent it toward a teammate in a vermilion bib. Along the fence, spectators sat on brick-red folding chairs beneath the reddish light of late afternoon. The ball moved between the teams while red sleeves crossed the faded white markings. At halftime, Beatriz drank from her bottle and adjusted a scarlet sock. After the final whistle, she folded her red jersey into her bag and walked past the rust-colored gate.

Bruno played midfield in an amateur football match on a municipal pitch. Before kickoff, he counted 7 players beside the touchline and 4 near the centre circle; 7 + 4 = 11, which completed his side. The referee set two halves of 30 minutes, and Bruno worked out that 2 × 30 = 60 minutes of play. After 18 minutes, he subtracted 18 from 60 and got 42 minutes remaining. During a stoppage, he counted 24 cones stacked in 6 equal piles beside the equipment shed; 24 ÷ 6 = 4 cones per pile. He then returned to his position. His side exchanged passes across the middle, and the opposing side intercepted one near the halfway line. Bruno covered the space behind the defender. At halftime, he moved a water bottle from the bench to the grass. The match resumed, with both sides continuing along the same marked boundaries until the final whistle.

Bruno played right back in an amateur football match on a municipal pitch beside a row of garages. Late in the second half, his clearance struck the crossbar, and a bolt dropped into the grass. The goalkeeper glanced upward. Bruno saw the left upright shift in its socket, then noticed a small child behind the net, tugging at a trapped ball. Another shot hit the frame. Metal groaned, and the whole goal tilted backward. Bruno's mouth went dry. He tried to call out, but his first breath produced nothing. The child remained crouched beneath the descending shadow. Bruno sprinted across the penalty area, his legs suddenly clumsy, his heartbeat pounding into his throat. He could already picture the crossbar striking that small head. “Move away,” he managed. The net caught his boot as he reached through it. He fell hard, grabbed the child's sleeve, and pulled while the bolts tore free overhead.

On Saturday afternoon, Priya stood beside the halfway line of a muddy football pitch behind the community centre. Her team had been trailing by a goal since the opening minutes, and her borrowed boots kept slipping on the grass. With only moments left, a teammate sent the ball across the field. Priya ran to meet it, steadied herself, and struck. The ball clipped the inside of the post and rolled into the net. For a heartbeat, she simply stared. Then her teammates reached her, arms swinging around her shoulders, and a laugh burst out of her so hard she could barely breathe. She bounced on her toes, grinning until her cheeks ached. They had drawn the match; her clumsy boots had carried her to the goal. Walking off the pitch, she kept replaying that clean strike in her head, and every replay made her break into another enormous smile.

Priya stood on the muddy touchline beside a row of school bags as the amateur football match entered its final ten minutes. Her team needed one goal, and she had spent the afternoon chasing passes across the battered pitch. When the ball finally reached her, she slipped between two defenders and struck it cleanly into the net. The referee blew his whistle and pointed the other way. Offside. She had been behind the ball when the pass came; even the opposing goalkeeper had seen it. Then she noticed the referee exchanging a grin with the defender who had tugged her shirt all afternoon. Heat climbed her neck. Her jaw locked, and her nails cut crescents into her palms. “You know that was a goal.” He waved her away without looking. Priya kicked a clump of turf hard enough to scatter mud across his shoes, then planted herself in front of him, refusing to move.

Priya arrived at the amateur football ground wearing a red jersey, crimson socks, and boots with burgundy laces. A brick-red clubhouse stood beside the pitch, where red cones marked the edges of the warmup area. She placed her scarlet kit bag beneath a bench and joined the players passing a white ball between red training poles. The referee wore a dark shirt and carried a red notebook in one pocket. During the first half, Priya received a pass near the touchline and sent the ball toward a teammate in a ruby vest. Beyond the fence, red buses crossed the road beneath the reddish light of late afternoon. At halftime, she drank from a red bottle while the substitutes arranged maroon jackets along the bench. The second half ended with the score unchanged on the red-framed board. Priya collected her scarlet bag, removed her crimson socks, and walked past the clubhouse toward the bus stop.

Priya played in an amateur football match on a council pitch bordered by hedges and a gravel path. Late in the second half, she chased a loose ball toward the goal while the goalkeeper rushed forward. Their shoulders collided, and she stumbled into the net. Behind her, metal scraped against concrete. The portable goal tilted as one of its unsecured feet lifted from the ground. She tried to step clear, but a loop of netting tightened around her boot. The crossbar moved above her, blotting out a strip of sky. Her mouth dried. She pulled once, twice, and only dragged herself backward beneath it. She pictured the bar striking her skull and could not make her fingers work on the knot. “Help me,” she said. Two players caught the frame while another tore the net from her ankle. Even after she crawled clear, her legs shook too hard to stand.

Hiroshi arrived at the neighborhood football field carrying his boots in a cloth bag. He sat on a bench, changed his shoes, and placed the bag beneath his jacket. Several players were passing a ball near the touchline. He joined them until the referee called everyone onto the field. Hiroshi took a position in midfield and watched the ball move between the defenders. When a teammate passed to him, he controlled it with his right foot and sent it toward the wing. The match continued with short passes, throw-ins, and occasional pauses while players retrieved the ball. At halftime, he drank water beside the bench and adjusted his socks. After play resumed, he followed an opposing player, intercepted a pass, and returned the ball to a teammate. When the referee ended the match, Hiroshi changed his shoes, folded his shirt, and walked toward the gate.

Priya arrived at the recreation ground carrying her boots in a cloth bag. She sat on a bench, changed her shoes, and placed the bag beneath her jacket. Several players passed a football across the grass while another set cones near the touchline. Priya joined the passing drill and then walked to her position for the amateur match. The referee checked the nets and blew the whistle. She received a pass near the halfway line, controlled the ball with the inside of her foot, and sent it toward a teammate. Play moved between the teams, with occasional throw-ins and stops for free kicks. During the interval, she drank water beside the bench and adjusted a sock. After play resumed, she covered a player near the wing and later took a throw-in. When the match ended, Priya collected her jacket, changed her shoes, and followed the path toward the gate.

Priya played midfield in an amateur football match on a municipal pitch. Before kickoff, she counted 7 players on each side and calculated 7 × 2 = 14 players altogether. Each team had 3 substitutes, so she added 14 + 6 = 20 people beside or on the field. The referee set two halves of 30 minutes; Priya multiplied 2 × 30 = 60 minutes of play. After 18 minutes, she subtracted 30 − 18 = 12 minutes remaining in the first half. She passed toward the touchline, moved between two markers, and received the ball again. At the interval, she divided 60 ÷ 4 = 15 while marking four equal sections on her match notes. The second half included several throw-ins and a change of goalkeeper. The match ended at 2 goals apiece. Priya added 2 + 2 = 4, recorded the total, and carried the cones into the equipment shed.

On Sunday afternoon, Hiroshi played midfield in an amateur football match on the municipal pitch beside the railway. With the score level, he carried the ball past two defenders and broke into the penalty area. A boot hooked his ankle from behind. He landed hard, scraping his palms, while the referee waved play on. Moments later, a slight shoulder challenge by Hiroshi earned a whistle and a yellow card. “That was nothing,” he said. The referee pointed him away without looking at the blood on his hands. Heat climbed his neck. His jaw locked, and he crushed the hem of his shirt between his fingers. The defender who had tripped him smirked behind the referee’s back. So that was how this match would be decided. Hiroshi stalked toward the restart, breathing sharply through his nose. When the ball came loose, he drove his foot through it, sending it rattling against the fence.

Priya arrived at the football pitch beside the harbor, where seawater moved between the pilings and fishing boats rested beyond the touchline. She placed her bag near a coil of rope and joined the amateur players as waves reached the seawall. The referee checked the nets while gulls crossed above the coastal road. Priya played in midfield, passing the ball across grass bordered by shells and patches of sand. Behind the opposite goal, the tide covered the lower steps of a landing used by small boats. A teammate sent her a short pass, and she redirected it toward the wing as a ferry crossed the bay. At halftime, she drank water beside the fence and watched crabs move through a shallow pool below the promenade. The second half ended with both teams level, while the harbor boats shifted against their moorings. Priya collected her bag and followed the coastline toward the bus stop.

Hiroshi played in an amateur football match on a grass pitch beside the harbor, where fishing boats rested beyond the touchline. The tide had reached the lower steps of the seawall when he took his position at midfield. Across the water, a ferry moved between two stretches of coastline while the referee checked both teams. Hiroshi received a pass, turned toward the sea-facing goal, and sent the ball along the grass to another player. Small waves folded against the harbor stones as the teams exchanged possession. During a break, he drank water beside a bucket containing shells collected from the beach. A gull crossed above the pitch while a substitute retrieved the ball near the coastal path. The match ended level, with the ferry returning past the breakwater. Hiroshi removed his boots, brushed away grass and sand, and walked along the seawall toward the harbor bus stop.

At two in the morning, Fatima stacked cartons beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights while rain tapped the loading doors. She had spent six hours clearing a backlog left by the previous shift, skipping her break to keep the conveyor moving. When the supervisor arrived, he pointed at three damaged boxes and told her their cost would come out of her pay. The torn packaging had been there when she clocked in; she had photographed it and filed a report. He waved away her phone without looking. “Your station, your responsibility.” Heat climbed her neck. Her jaw tightened until a tooth ached, and the scanner creaked in her grip. He had signed that report himself. Now he stood between her and the office, tapping his watch. Fatima set the scanner down with deliberate care, forwarded the photographs to payroll, and demanded that he put the deduction in writing. She would not spend another minute making his numbers look clean.

On Sunday afternoon, Hiroshi stood at midfield on a muddy park pitch while two amateur football teams lined up beneath a row of bare trees. His side had trailed by a goal since halftime, and his last two passes had rolled straight to opponents. With seconds remaining, a teammate sent the ball skidding toward him. Hiroshi trapped it, stepped around a defender, and struck with the foot he usually trusted only for standing. The ball clipped the post and crossed the line. Before he could turn, his teammates were running toward him, arms spread. A laugh burst from his chest. He bounced on his toes as they crowded around, their muddy hands thumping his back. Somewhere behind them, the referee blew for full time. Hiroshi kept replaying that clean strike in his head. Even while collecting the cones afterward, he grinned so broadly that his cheeks ached, and every few steps became a little skip.

At midnight, Fatima stood beside a conveyor belt in the warehouse, sorting parcels beneath fluorescent lights. Her phone vibrated inside her vest just as she lifted a box marked FRAGILE. The hospital number appeared on the screen. She pulled off one glove with her teeth and answered. “She’s gone,” a nurse said. Fatima kept the box suspended between the belt and the trolley until her wrists began to shake. That afternoon, she had promised her mother she would visit after work; she had even packed the soft pears her mother could still eat. Now they sat in her locker, ripening for nobody. She lowered the box carefully, as though breaking anything else might finish her. Around her, scanners chirped and cartons slid past. She pressed her bare palm against the cold metal trolley and tried to remember the last thing her mother had said. All she could hear was herself saying tomorrow.

On Sunday afternoon, Hiroshi played midfield in an amateur football match on a grass pitch behind the school. Late in the second half, his shot struck the crossbar, and the portable goal rocked backward. One of its anchoring pegs sprang from the ground. A small child ducked behind the net to retrieve the ball just as a gust caught the mesh. Hiroshi saw the rear support rise and the heavy crossbar begin tipping forward. His stomach clenched. For a moment his legs would not move; he could already picture the metal striking the child’s skull. Then he sprinted, his mouth dry, his breath scraping his throat. “Get out,” he shouted. The child turned but caught a shoe in the net. Hiroshi grabbed the crossbar with both hands. Its weight dragged him to his knees. Other players reached him and lifted together. After the child crawled clear, Hiroshi still could not make his fingers release the cold metal.

On Sunday afternoon, Priya’s amateur football team played on a muddy pitch behind the village hall. Her father stood beside the touchline, holding the flask he brought to every match. When she scored, she looked towards him before looking at the net. He raised one hand, then folded to the ground. Priya ran across the white line without waiting for the whistle. Someone called an ambulance; someone else pressed steadily against his chest. She knelt beside his boots, staring at a loose lace she could not bring herself to tie. At the hospital, a doctor said, “We couldn’t save him.” She still had mud on her knees. Her phone kept lighting up with messages about the winning goal, and she turned it facedown. Later, she found his flask in her kit bag. Two cups were tucked beneath its lid. She set both on the kitchen table and sat until the room went dark.

Hiroshi played midfield in an amateur football match on a grass pitch beside a row of sheds. Before kickoff, he counted 11 players on each side and calculated 11 + 11 = 22 players altogether. The referee set two halves of 35 minutes, and Hiroshi worked out 35 × 2 = 70 minutes of play. During the first half, he received six passes from one teammate and four from another, noting that 6 + 4 = 10. At halftime, he checked the water bottles: 18 had been placed beside the bench, and seven had been used, so 18 − 7 = 11 remained. Four substitute players shared 12 orange slices; he calculated 12 ÷ 4 = 3 slices each. He returned to midfield, intercepted a rolling pass, and sent the ball toward the touchline. The match ended at 1–1. Hiroshi collected three cones from each of four corners, making 3 × 4 = 12, and stacked them beside the equipment bag.

Hiroshi arrived at the amateur football ground wearing a red jersey, with crimson socks folded above his boots. Beside the touchline, a scarlet canvas bag held his water bottle and a spare shirt. The teams stood near red corner flags while an unnamed referee checked the ball and his watch. Hiroshi took his position beneath the rust-red roof of the small spectator stand. During the opening minutes, he passed toward a teammate whose burgundy sleeves reached his wrists. The ball crossed the grass, rolled beside a red-painted boundary post, and returned through midfield. At halftime, Hiroshi sat on a vermilion bench and drank from his red bottle. Crimson sunlight spread across the stand as the second half continued. He took a throw-in beside a scarlet equipment cart, then moved back into position. The match ended level, and Hiroshi changed behind a red wooden screen before leaving through the brick-red gate.

At two in the morning, Fatima scanned cartons beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights while rain tapped the loading doors. A metal shriek came from the next aisle, followed by a crash that rattled the floor. She lowered her scanner. At the far end of her aisle, a forklift had struck a rack support, bending it toward the shelves. The driver climbed out and ran toward the loading bay. Above Fatima, stacked pallets shifted, and a bolt struck the concrete beside her shoe. She backed toward the emergency exit, but a fallen carton blocked the handle. Her fingers slipped against the smooth cardboard. Another bolt dropped. The rack leaned farther, its highest boxes tilting over her head. She tried to call out, but only a thin breath escaped. If the shelving fell, nobody would reach her in time. She crouched behind a concrete pillar, pressed both hands over her skull, and waited for the next crash.

Hiroshi stood beside the chalk touchline while eleven players in mismatched shirts gathered on the municipal pitch. It was their last amateur match before the ground became a car park. His father had helped mark those lines for thirty years, and Hiroshi wore the boots they had chosen together before the hospital visits began. With the score level, a teammate passed him the ball six yards from goal. He struck the post. The rebound rolled away, and the final whistle followed.

Around him, players exchanged handshakes and collected cones. Hiroshi remained near the goal, staring at the small dent his shot had left in the paint. He had imagined scoring once more here, giving this place an ending his father might have applauded. Now there would be no next week. He knelt to untie his boots, but his fingers slipped against the laces. When the groundskeeper lifted the corner flag, Hiroshi pressed both palms into the grass and could not stand.

Fatima entered the warehouse through the side door and placed her coat in a locker. She clipped a scanner to her belt, collected a cart, and walked toward the shelving beneath the overhead lights. The night shift followed the posted schedule. She scanned labels on cartons, moved packages onto the cart, and took them to the packing station. A worker at the next table folded boxes while another pushed a pallet jack along the marked aisle. Fatima sealed each carton with tape and attached its shipping label. Between batches, she cleared scraps from the tabletop and put an empty roll into the recycling bin. During her break, she sat beside a vending machine and drank water from her bottle. She returned to the station, stacked the remaining cartons, and wiped the scanner with a cloth. At the end of the shift, she returned the cart and retrieved her coat.

At midnight, Fatima worked beneath the warehouse’s strip lights, sorting cartons beside a conveyor belt. The last truck waited outside, but a missing pallet had stopped the shipment, and the supervisor was checking the clock. Fatima walked the aisles again, following the inventory numbers with her finger. Behind a stack of empty crates, she spotted a label facing the wall. She pulled the crates aside. There it was: every missing carton, wrapped and ready. “Found it,” she called. The crew moved quickly, and the pallet rolled into the truck with three minutes remaining. When the driver lowered the door, Fatima’s shoulders lifted as if the weight had come off her own back. She laughed, pressed both hands over her mouth, then laughed again. Her coworkers tapped their knuckles against hers. For the rest of the shift, she practically bounced between stations, replaying that glimpse of the label, amazed that her small discovery had made everything click into place.

Fatima began her night shift beneath red ceiling panels that tinted the warehouse aisles a muted brick shade. She placed her lunch container in a burgundy locker and clipped a scarlet badge to her gray shirt. At the packing station, she counted twelve rolls of red tape beside a stack of cartons printed with maroon squares. Her first pallet held crimson fabric, folded into rectangles and wrapped in clear sheets. She scanned each label, entered the quantities, and moved the bundles onto a trolley with red wheels. Near midnight, an unnamed coworker left a terracotta mug beside the inventory terminal. Fatima drank water from her own red bottle, then checked the shelf numbers against a russet folder. The overhead clock had cherry-colored hands, which advanced while she sorted another carton of red ribbon. Before dawn, she parked the trolley within a red rectangle painted on the floor and returned the burgundy clipboard to its hook.

Fatima began her night shift at the warehouse beside a pallet of sealed cartons. She counted 28 cartons on one rack and 17 on another, then wrote 28 + 17 = 45 on the inventory sheet. Of those 45 cartons, 9 belonged in the loading area, so she calculated 45 − 9 = 36 and marked the remaining stock. Each carton contained 6 packets; she multiplied 36 × 6 = 216 before checking the shelf labels. She divided the packets among 12 storage bins, recording 216 ÷ 12 = 18 packets per bin. At midnight, she measured a row of 8 pallets, each 120 centimeters long, and entered 8 × 120 = 960 centimeters in the aisle log. A worker brought another sheet. Fatima checked its total of 14 + 23 = 37, clipped it beneath the inventory page, and continued scanning cartons under the overhead lights.

Fatima worked the night shift in a warehouse beside the harbor, where seawater rose against the quay beneath the loading doors. She checked cartons of ship fittings while waves tapped the stone wall outside. A printed tide table lay beside her scanner, its columns marked with the heights for the neighboring coastline. She moved a pallet of coiled rope into a numbered bay as a cargo ship crossed the channel beyond the windows. At midnight, she recorded the arrival of crates containing glass floats and nets used along the coast. Another worker stacked empty trays near a tank where mussels filtered circulating seawater. Fatima counted the trays, entered the total, and returned to the shelves of marine supplies. During her break, she ate bread beside a window overlooking anchored boats and the exposed tidal flats. Before dawn, she signed the ledger while the incoming tide covered the harbor steps.

Malik began his night shift at the warehouse beside a row of stacked cartons. He counted 24 boxes on one pallet and 18 on another, then wrote 24 + 18 = 42 on the inventory sheet. At the next rack, he subtracted 7 cartons removed earlier from the original 35, recording 35 - 7 = 28. Each carton held 12 packets, so he calculated 28 × 12 = 336 packets. He divided those packets among 8 storage bins and noted 336 ÷ 8 = 42 packets per bin. The overhead lights remained on while a forklift passed through the adjoining aisle. Malik measured a shelf with 180 centimeters of usable space. Since each container occupied 30 centimeters, he worked out 180 ÷ 30 = 6 containers. He placed six containers along the shelf, entered the figures into the terminal, and wheeled the empty cart toward the loading bay.

At midnight, Malik worked beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights, stacking cartons beside a loading bay. He had spent six hours clearing a shipment that two absent workers should have handled. When the supervisor arrived, he pointed at the remaining pallets and tapped his watch. “You're staying until it's finished.” Malik reminded him that his overtime from last week still hadn't been paid. The supervisor shrugged and crossed Malik’s completed loads off the tally sheet, assigning them to someone who had left before supper. Heat climbed Malik’s neck. His molars pressed together until his jaw ached, and the carton in his hands buckled beneath his thumbs. Six hours erased with a pen. He set the crushed box down, slowly enough that nobody could call it throwing. Then he pulled the tally sheet toward him and photographed it. His fingers shook, but he kept the camera steady for the second picture, where the alterations showed clearly.

Malik began his night shift beneath red ceiling lamps, with a crimson clipboard tucked against his gray shirt. He crossed the warehouse floor between pallets wrapped in red film and stacks of burgundy cartons. At the packing table, he matched scarlet labels to item numbers and entered each quantity in a ledger with a red cover. A worker pushed a maroon trolley past him, carrying rolls of ruby fabric toward the loading bay. Malik placed six red plastic containers inside a larger box and sealed its edges with brick-colored tape. During the scheduled break, he sat beside a red vending machine and drank water from a clear bottle with a cherry-colored cap. Afterward, he counted crimson spools on the lower shelves while red light stretched across the concrete. At four, he returned the clipboard to its red hook, recorded the final total, and carried another burgundy carton to the sorting table.

At two in the morning, Malik worked the warehouse night shift beneath fluorescent lights, scanning cartons beside a row of steel racks. A pallet scraped overhead, although the forklift stood parked across the aisle. He looked up. One support beam had bent outward, and boxes on the highest shelf were inching toward its edge. Then a bolt struck the concrete beside his shoe. Malik dropped the scanner and backed away, but the rack behind him blocked the narrow passage. His pulse hammered against his collar. The nearest exit lay beyond the leaning shelves; reaching it meant passing underneath them. Another bolt snapped loose. He pictured the morning crew finding his flattened badge among the cartons. His hands shook so badly that he missed the radio button twice. As the steel began to groan, he crawled beneath a packing table, pressed his forehead against his knees, and listened to the first pallet fall.

At two in the morning, Malik moved cartons beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights while rain tapped the loading doors. His phone vibrated against his thigh as he scanned a box of kitchen stools. The hospital number appeared on the screen. He answered with one hand still resting on the cardboard, and a nurse told him his father had died eleven minutes earlier. Malik looked at the timestamp on his scanner. Eleven minutes ago, he had been correcting a shipment label. He tried to ask whether anyone had been beside the bed, but his throat closed around the question. After the call, he carried the same carton halfway down three different aisles. A supervisor took it from him and pointed toward the break room. There, Malik opened the lunch his father had packed that afternoon. Two sandwiches, cut diagonally. He touched one corner until the bread flattened, then bent over the table, unable to swallow or leave it.

At midnight, Malik stood beside a conveyor belt in the warehouse while rain tapped the loading-bay roof. The last truck waited outside, and thirty cartons still needed labels before the driver’s departure. When the printer jammed, Malik opened its cover and found a strip of backing paper wound around a roller. He eased it free, fed in a fresh sheet, and watched the first clean barcode emerge. Soon cartons slid past his hands in a steady stream. He scanned the final box with four minutes remaining. His supervisor checked the shipment, then handed him an envelope: confirmation of the permanent position he had been working toward for months. Malik read it twice. A laugh burst from his chest, and he bounced on his heels before catching himself. He pictured telling his mother over breakfast, pictured rent paid without counting every coin. Even the wet walk to the bus seemed worth celebrating.

Malik began his night shift at the warehouse beside the harbor, where seawater reached the stone steps beneath the loading platform. He checked cartons of dried seaweed against a clipboard while fishing boats moved across the dark water beyond the windows. The warehouse clock marked midnight as he stacked rope, folded sailcloth, and sealed boxes of brass fittings for ships offshore. Between pallets, a narrow drain carried traces of seawater toward the quay, and he swept loose packing fibers away from its grate. At the next loading bay, an unnamed driver delivered crates of oysters harvested along the coastline. Malik recorded their weight, wheeled them into the cold room, and returned the empty trolley beside a bundle of fishing nets. During his break, he ate bread at a table overlooking the tide and the anchored vessels. Before dawn, he counted the remaining cargo while small waves tapped the harbor wall outside.

Malik arrived at the warehouse after sunset and hung his jacket on a hook beside the time clock. He scanned his badge, collected a handheld scanner, and walked to the loading area. Pallets stood along the marked lanes, with shipping labels attached to the outer wrapping. He checked each label against the list on his screen and moved a cart toward the shelving. An unnamed coworker passed with an empty pallet jack. Malik placed several cartons on the cart, pushed it down the aisle, and transferred them to their assigned shelves. The overhead lights stayed on throughout the building. Near the loading doors, a ventilation fan ran above a stack of folded cartons. During his break, he sat at a table and ate a sandwich from his bag. He then returned to the aisle, scanned the remaining cartons, and left the cart beside the supply cabinet before his shift ended.

At midnight, Agnes stood beside the loading belt in a warehouse lit by fluorescent strips. She had spent six hours clearing a backlog while the supervisor sat upstairs, watching videos on his phone. When the final pallet rolled through, he handed her a warning slip for missing her packing quota. The hours unloading his overdue delivery did not count, he said, and the warning would cost her next week's overtime.

“Sign it.”

Heat climbed her neck. Agnes looked at his clean cuffs, then at the split skin beneath her own gloves. He had ordered her off the packing line; now he was charging her for obeying. Her jaw tightened until her teeth ached. She pressed the pen so hard against the clipboard that its plastic clip snapped. Then she wrote the unloading times across the signature box, demanded a copy, and planted herself in the office doorway until he made one.

Agnes arrived at the warehouse after sunset and placed her coat in a locker beside the staff entrance. She checked the assignment sheet, collected a scanner, and walked to the packing benches. Overhead lights shone on cardboard boxes and rolls of tape. She scanned each label, folded the box flaps, and pressed tape along the seams. An unnamed worker brought another trolley and parked it beside her bench. Agnes moved the finished cartons onto a pallet, keeping the labels facing outward. During her break, she sat at a table near the vending machine and drank water from a bottle. Then she returned to the floor and replaced an empty tape roll. Beyond the loading doors, a truck stood beneath the yard lights. Near the end of her shift, she wiped the bench, returned the scanner to its charging rack, collected her coat, and left through the staff entrance.

At two in the morning, Agnes worked between stacked pallets beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights. She scanned the last carton on her trolley when a metallic crash came from the loading bay. The overhead lights blinked out, leaving only the red exit signs. Somewhere beyond the shelving, an engine started. Agnes stepped toward the aisle and saw a forklift rolling backward without anyone in its seat. Its raised forks caught a rack support. Steel buckled, and boxes began dropping from the highest shelf. She ran for the nearest exit, but a fallen pallet blocked the door. Another support snapped behind her. Her hands shook so badly that she dropped her radio twice. The racks leaned toward one another, passing the collapse down the aisle. Agnes crawled beneath her trolley, pulled her knees against her chest, and watched the ceiling disappear behind falling cartons. She could not stop imagining the next shelf landing across her spine.

Agnes began her night shift at the warehouse beside a stack of shipping sheets. She counted 28 cartons on one pallet and 17 on another, then wrote 28 + 17 = 45 in the inventory log. From a row of 63 containers, she removed 19 for sorting and recorded 63 − 19 = 44. Each rack held 8 trays, so the 6 racks along the wall contained 6 × 8 = 48 trays. She divided 72 labels among 9 bins and entered 72 ÷ 9 = 8 labels per bin. The overhead lights remained on while she moved between the shelves and the loading area. At the packing bench, she measured three strips of tape at 24 centimeters each, making 3 × 24 = 72 centimeters. She placed the completed sheets in a folder, returned the measuring tool to its drawer, and checked the next pallet against its printed list.

At midnight, Agnes stood beside the loading belt in a warehouse lined with stacked cartons and humming fluorescent lights. The last truck waited outside, but a jam had stopped the belt with forty orders still unpacked. She crouched beneath the rollers, found a torn shipping label wound around a spindle, and worked it loose with her pocket scissors. When the belt shuddered forward, she sprang up and waved the packers back to their stations. Boxes slid into waiting hands. Tape snapped, scanners chirped, and the pile dwindled until the final carton disappeared through the loading door. The driver raised a thumb from the cab. Agnes checked the departure clock: three minutes early. A laugh burst out of her, and she pressed both palms against her cheeks. They had done it. Every waiting household would get its parcel tomorrow. She practically bounced toward the time clock, her tired legs suddenly light, replaying that raised thumb with every step.

Agnes began her night shift beneath the warehouse’s red ceiling lamps, wearing a brick-red vest over her gray uniform. She collected a crimson clipboard from the desk and followed the red floor stripe toward the loading bays. Pallets wrapped in translucent ruby film stood beside stacks of scarlet plastic crates. She compared the printed quantities with the cartons, marking each row with a red pencil. At midnight, an unnamed worker brought another pallet on a maroon hand truck and placed its paperwork in the red tray. Agnes entered the numbers at a terminal with a burgundy keyboard cover. During her scheduled break, she ate rice from a red container beside the warehouse’s garnet-painted lockers. Then she returned to the aisles, where red fabric rolls occupied the lower shelves. Before dawn, she stacked the completed sheets beneath a vermilion paperweight, hung her vest on a red hook, and left through the brick-red door.

Agnes began her night shift at the warehouse beside the harbor, where seawater lifted fishing boats against their mooring ropes. She checked a manifest of net floats while small waves passed beneath the loading pier. Along the open doorway, the coastline appeared as a row of lamps above the tide. Agnes moved cartons of dried seaweed onto a pallet and recorded their weights in the ledger. A worker brought in crates of empty oyster shells, their surfaces carrying traces of saltwater and sand. At midnight, she ate bread beside a window overlooking a cargo ship anchored beyond the harbor wall. The tide receded while she counted coils of rope intended for coastal trawlers. Before dawn, Agnes swept scattered shell fragments from the concrete floor and secured the doors facing the sea. She entered the final inventory figures as gulls crossed above the water and the next shift arrived from the waterfront road.

At midnight, Agnes stood beside a conveyor belt in the warehouse, beneath fluorescent tubes and rows of cardboard cartons. She scanned parcels, turned their labels upward, and stacked them on a pallet. Her phone vibrated inside her vest. The hospital number appeared, and she stepped between two shelves to answer. A nurse told her that her mother had died minutes earlier. Agnes kept pressing the phone against her ear after the call ended, listening to the empty line. That afternoon, she had promised to visit after her shift; she had even packed the soft biscuits her mother could still manage. Now the little packet in her locker had nowhere to go. She returned to the belt and lifted a carton, but her fingers opened before she could set it down. Kneeling among spilled envelopes, she could not catch her breath. She gathered one envelope, then another, while tears darkened the concrete between her knees.

At midnight, Dmitri worked beneath the warehouse strip lights while rain tapped the loading bay roof. A truck waited outside, and twelve pallets still needed labels before the morning shipments could leave. Then the printer jammed. He opened its casing, eased out a crumpled strip, and found the loose roller that had stalled it all week. With a borrowed screwdriver, he tightened the bracket and fed the paper through again. Labels streamed into his hands, crisp and straight. He laughed, a sudden sound that bounced between the racks. His shoulders lifted; his tired feet began keeping time with the printer. Each finished pallet felt like another door swinging open. When the driver scanned the last label and gave him a thumbs-up, Dmitri grinned so widely his cheeks ached. They had made the deadline with seven minutes to spare. He rubbed his palms together, already imagining breakfast in the first daylight, with nothing unfinished behind him.

At midnight, Dmitri stood beside the loading conveyor beneath the warehouse’s fluorescent lights. He had spent six hours correcting mislabeled pallets while the supervisor smoked outside. When the final truck arrived, the supervisor handed him a written warning for the delay and crossed two hours off his time sheet. “You should have worked faster.” Dmitri stared at the altered numbers. He had skipped his break; he had hauled every damaged crate alone. Now the man who had given him the wrong shipping list was taking money from his pocket. Heat climbed his neck.
